pages.title: Forestry road planning
pages.subtitle: For forestry teams evaluating road access and design options: the workflow, the current capabilities, the data preparation a pilot needs, and the options for configuration or further development.

blocks.title: Terrain, geometry, sections and cost assumptions *in one browser workspace.*
blocks.lead: A forester can move from a mapped block or an initial corridor to editable road alternatives, inspect the ground beneath them, and produce a review package that explains how the results were obtained. [1]

blocks.alt: Live DDC Access workspace on the published native 1 m BC LiDAR terrain. The alignment and entered engineering assumptions are illustrative and require review. Screen captured 14 November 2026.
blocks.label: Figure 1
blocks.caption: Live DDC Access workspace on the published native 1 m BC LiDAR terrain. The alignment and entered engineering assumptions are illustrative and require review. Screen captured 14 November 2026.

blocks.text: The product is suited to preliminary planning, option comparison and geometric design. Its practical value is the ability to examine a change in the plan alongside its profile, section, quantities and assumptions. Existing LiDAR import and terrain-preparation tools allow a project to develop beyond regional screening when more suitable ground information is available. [1,2]

This paper explains the workflow, the current capabilities, the data preparation needed for a customer pilot, and the options for configuration or further development. It is intended for foresters, road planners, consultants and managers deciding whether to trial DDC Access on a representative project.

blocks.title: A workflow for a forestry decision
blocks.lead: Begin with the block or landing that needs access and the roads and constraints that could affect it. DDC Access can search BC records by opening, licence, cutting permit, timber mark or block identifier. Access investigation keeps source records visible before a design is introduced. [3]

blocks.alt: BC access investigation in the live application. Mapped block and road records support investigation; their presence does not establish a constructed, serviceable or authorized access route. Screen captured 14 November 2026.
blocks.label: Figure 2
blocks.caption: BC access investigation in the live application. Mapped block and road records support investigation; their presence does not establish a constructed, serviceable or authorized access route. Screen captured 14 November 2026.

blocks.text: Screen the access problem

Review mapped roads, harvest history, possible entrances and crossing context. Record what is known about existing access and identify what needs a field check. Regional terrain can support broad corridor screening where suitable LiDAR has not yet been prepared. Keep its terrain label with the discussion and results. [1,3,4]
Develop and compare a road

Start from mapped linework, peg or sketch a new alignment, or generate bounded alternatives. Refine horizontal geometry and the independent vertical design, then examine sections and quantities on the same chainage. Use common assumptions to explain differences. [1,4]
Prepare the review

Save the editable project with its terrain and assumptions, then export the relevant drawings, quantities and geometry. Record the preferred option, the reasons for it and the remaining field questions. The project team determines the required professional design and approvals. [1,10,15]

blocks.title: Connected views and editable geometry
blocks.lead: Road decisions become easier to discuss when the views refer to the same place.

blocks.text: Selecting a station in DDC Access links the plan, longitudinal profile, cross-section, mass curve and station schedule. The 3D view adds an orbit or follow-station perspective. Moving the camera changes presentation without changing the analytical terrain or road quantities. [1]

blocks.text: The template and assembly tools accommodate more than one uniform section. Users can manage left and right components, transitions, material layers and station-specific assignments. That matters where a route changes from a cut section to fill, passes a landing, or needs a local width adjustment. The displayed results still depend on entered geometry and on sufficient terrain across the section. [1,5]

Route assistance can test terrain, grades, exclusion clearances, stream-crossing preferences and reviewed existing-road reuse assumptions. Other corridor and profile tools have their own objectives. They should be treated as ways to develop candidates, with their settings and scope read before comparison. A bounded search can fail because of its search limits; that does not establish that no professional solution exists. [4]

A forester can retain alternatives and explain why one is preferable. The comparison is strongest when all candidates use the same terrain reference, section conventions, material definitions and cost basis. The application makes those inputs editable; the pilot should establish the organization's accepted starting values. [1,4,6]

blocks.title: Costs that retain their assumptions
blocks.lead: DDC Access offers several cost views because different decisions need different levels of detail. These values should be named accurately in a proposal or meeting. [1,6]

rows: Route screening
Entered route penalties and preferences for candidate generation.
Find corridors worth reviewing.
Engineering estimate
Supported sections and quantities, materials, structures and entered rates.
Compare the work implied by a defined road option.
Complete access cost
New-road work plus reviewed connected access, source supply, haul, return paths and selected allowances.
Compare a finite set of fully priced, checked alternatives.

blocks.text: A preliminary route-search score is useful for generating options. A geometric estimate relates entered rates to calculated work. A complete access comparison adds reviewed existing-road and material-supply paths. The engineering workflow records excavation and fill, material horizons, conversion assumptions, stripping, surfacing, clearing, culverts and haul inputs. Material allocation distinguishes quantities such as bank and compacted volumes. Missing ground or unfinished daylight is visible; an incomplete section does not become a complete quantity merely because its road surface is drawn. [1,5,7]
Account for access and material supply

A low acquisition price does not make material free to use. Complete access costing can include processing, loading, placement, source preparation, loaded haul and empty return. Each source needs an entrance, availability, capacity and applicable prices. A disconnected pit cannot be supplied through an invented straight-line path. [6,8]

Reused roads carry entered access, condition, season, vehicle and structure restrictions. The network can retain separate outward and return paths and apply shared road or source allowances once. A comparison only prices an alternative as feasible when the required geometry, quantities, connectivity, capacity and prices pass its checks. Unknown costs remain unknown. [6,8]
Keep a quote connected to its crossing

Stream crossing estimates record a chosen structure type, quantities, rates, references and price dates. A changed physical crossing requires renewed geometry review. Shared work can be accounted for once per alternative, and an existing culvert allowance can be explicitly replaced to avoid competing amounts. [9]

Default rates are placeholders. Use attributable local quotes and test sensitivity to haul, rehabilitation and supply assumptions. The comparison is a finite planning estimate, not a global optimum or contractor bid. [1,6,9]

blocks.title: LiDAR is part of the current workflow
blocks.lead: LiDAR support is already available. The published example uses a native 1 m bare-earth digital terrain model for BC tile 093G086, acquired in July 2024. Its source and product checksums are recorded. [1,2,11]

blocks.text: The application can also import a customer's GeoTIFF or LAS/LAZ corridor and use its resulting ground surface in the road workflow. A better ground dataset can reveal terrain variation that a coarse regional surface cannot represent. DDC Access reads analytical elevations from the terrain source, rather than from the displayed contours or 3D mesh. Profiles, sections and quantities therefore remain tied to the selected ground and its missing-data footprint. Cell spacing describes the grid; it does not certify vertical accuracy. [1,11]

rows: Bare-earth GeoTIFF
Preserve native cells and no-data; require a named vertical reference.
LAS or LAZ
Use existing ground classes, classify when absent, or reclassify; choose ground means or TIN.
Known terrain detail
Import breaklines; preserve input point density around the road corridor.
Adjacent sources
Mosaic compatible rasters or combine compatible point clouds with recorded provenance.
Prepared surface
Retain and edit TIN elevations; grade a pad; combine a road surface for a junction.
Additional context
Display canopy-height or orthophoto backgrounds independently of analytical ground.

blocks.text: These choices allow a pilot to begin with a supplied bare-earth raster and add more detailed processing where it changes the decision. The team should inspect classification, breakline handling, gaps and overlap precedence rather than assuming that a successful import validates the terrain. A background canopy or image layer adds context but never supplies missing ground elevations. [2]

The provincial LidarBC program provides open access to LiDAR and related products, including LAZ data, as coverage is acquired, processed and released. Availability should be checked for the project area. A local collection, survey delivery or externally prepared corridor may be the appropriate input. [13,14]

blocks.title: A practical LiDAR intake and review
blocks.lead: Six steps from a delivered dataset to an accepted project that reopens the same way.

items.title: Define the corridor and purpose
items.text: Choose a manageable project area that includes the proposed alignment, section reach, possible tie-ins and any alternatives. Specify whether the task is corridor reconnaissance, preliminary quantities or comparison with a surveyed design. That decision determines the ground support and checking effort needed.

items.title: Establish the source
items.text: Record the provider, acquisition date, classification method, horizontal coordinate system, height reference, units and relevant accuracy information. Confirm that a raster is bare earth. The published sample tile uses NAD83(CSRS) UTM zone 10N and CGVD2013 heights; a customer delivery may differ. DDC Access records a vertical reference but does not convert between height datums. [1,11]

items.title: Prepare a supported input
items.text: Crop and, where necessary, reproject externally to a supported north-up raster or compatible point cloud. Road-design GeoTIFF imports are bounded at 64 MB and 4,194,304 native cells. Combined point-cloud imports accept up to twelve files and 1 GB total, subject to point, grid and memory limits. Large deliveries should be prepared as representative corridors before onboarding. [1,2]

items.title: Select and document processing
items.text: For a point cloud, decide whether source ground classes are suitable. Choose a ground-mean grid or TIN, add checked breaklines where needed, and set any corridor-preservation width. Compatible ground sources can be mosaicked with an explicit overlap choice. The project records source identities and processing choices; repeat processing still requires the original inputs. [2]

items.title: Review support and geometry
items.text: Inspect hillshade and terrain overlays for spikes, vegetation retained as ground, sparse-ground facets and gaps. Confirm that the ground covers both sides of the road. Compare selected sample elevations and sections against independently trusted checks, using a tolerance agreed for the pilot. A 3D display patch or attractive contour does not resolve analytical missing data. [1,11]

items.title: Recalculate and hand off
items.text: Revisit the route and vertical controls against the accepted terrain. Recalculate quantities and costs, inspect incomplete stations, then export the selected geometry, surfaces, schedules and project. Confirm the exported coordinate and height references in the receiving application. A successful pilot should reproduce the same accepted project after save and reopen. [1,2,10]

blocks.title: Access and environmental context
blocks.lead: Existing access often determines whether a proposed route is useful. DDC Access separates a road record from a reviewed reuse assumption.

blocks.text: The connected-network workflow can retain actual path geometry, declared junctions, entrance attachments, road condition observations and vehicle or structure restrictions. Crossed map lines do not automatically become a physical junction. [3,8]

This distinction is valuable during a desktop review. A team can identify an apparent connection, record the evidence still needed and test an explicit scenario without presenting the assumption as a field observation. Dated condition and bridge-rating evidence can inform the chosen network policy. The reviewer fields are entered assertions, rather than authenticated professional credentials. [8]

blocks.alt: Synthetic training example: stream review band, exclusion area and drainage controls after a drainage check. Run results need review; this is not a completed hydraulic design.
blocks.label: Figure 4
blocks.caption: Synthetic training example: stream review band, exclusion area and drainage controls after a drainage check. Run results need review; this is not a completed hydraulic design.

blocks.text: Bring assessed constraints into the design

Stream lines, crossing records and exclusion areas support route review. Import assessed riparian areas, wetlands or other protected polygons and set the treatment required by the project. A buffer around an unclassified stream centreline does not establish a riparian classification, fish presence or permission to cross. Structure selection and crossing prices remain explicit inputs. [4,9]

The terrain and drainage tools help examine geometry and flow context. They do not replace site hydrology, fish-passage assessment, geotechnical work or an engineered structure design. Use the results to focus the questions that must be resolved and retain those questions in the review record. [1,9,15]
Extend the conversation to related LiDAR tools

The wider platform also includes a separate LiDAR workbench for original point-cloud and derived terrain or canopy inspection. A browser restoration and stand-structure workspace processes classified clouds into ground, slope, height and return-distribution products. Its terrain GeoTIFF can be imported into Road design. [11,12]

These modules extend the product conversation beyond the road centreline, while their output names retain their meaning. Crown candidates are not verified stems or species; return-height metrics are not measured timber volume or restoration suitability. The appropriate module and validation effort depend on the question the customer needs to answer. [11,12]

blocks.title: Configure the product around the operation
blocks.lead: The first customization step is to agree which decisions recur in the organization. Many can be represented through current project inputs and reusable libraries. Other requests require a scoped integration or new development. [1,2,5,10]

Import supported terrain, spatial context, breaklines and imagery.
Prepare deliveries, add source connectors or automate a processing pipeline.
Road standards
Named templates, components, material libraries, station assignments and transitions.
Package and validate organization-specific standard libraries.
Planning assumptions
Grade, radius, exclusion and stream settings; reviewed existing-road preferences.
Implement additional project rules with defined tests and review owners.
Costs and supply
Rates, material factors, sources, capacities, entrances, haul and rehabilitation.
Connect approved quote or costing data; agree refresh and provenance rules.
Review presentation
Layouts, visible panels, plot-book chapters, ranges, scales and output selection.
Report branding, additional schedules or specific customer handoff formats.
Organization operations

Scope identity, permissions, shared cloud projects, hosting and support if required.

blocks.text: Keeping those categories explicit makes a pilot easier to evaluate and a later proposal easier to price. Configuration should be tested against a realistic sample. For example, a template library is useful only if its transitions and resulting sections behave as expected on the customer's terrain. A source connector is useful only if its identifiers, coverage and update rules preserve the meaning of the records. The pilot can establish those requirements before a broader rollout.

LiDAR extension does not need to begin with a new analysis service. A practical first scope is a checked corridor dataset, an agreed preparation record, a sample design and exports that open correctly in the receiving GIS. A larger-area pipeline, additional analytical methods or survey-quality integration can follow when their need is demonstrated.

blocks.label: Commercial terms
blocks.text: Commercial terms should be based on the accepted scope, data responsibilities, support expectations and deployment arrangement. This white paper does not assume a licence price, service level or measured return on investment.

blocks.title: Interoperability and operating boundaries
blocks.lead: DDC Access supports open files so a preliminary decision can continue into other tools. Choose the output for the next task and retain the editable project when full design state matters. [1,10]

rows: Project JSON
Portable editable project, terrain/provenance and saved assumptions; principal restoration format.
GeoJSON and shapefile
Roads, stations and selected context for GIS review and spatial exchange.
LandXML
Design alignment/profile/sections and terrain surface handoff in their declared reference systems.
CSV schedules
Stations, sections, engineering/material quantities, haul movements and related review fields.
PDF and printable reports
Map and report PDF, HTML report and configurable A3/A4 plot books for discussion.

Square-cell ground exchange and reusable template/material definitions.

blocks.text: Exported line geometry alone does not reconstruct every template, vertical control, material input or cost record.
Check the receiving application

Import a representative export into the customer's GIS or design system and compare location, height reference, units, geometry and sample quantities. Native RoadEng or DWG project compatibility is not established by an open-format export. Survey reduction and stakeout CSV also have a narrower scope than a complete instrument-specific construction package. [1,2,10]
Plan for persistence and coverage

The project library and autosave use browser-local storage. A downloaded project provides the portable handoff across devices or browsers; storage quotas and large embedded rasters should be checked during the pilot. Network-dependent basemaps and source data have their own availability. An embedded imported terrain can be reopened without fetching it again. [1,10]

Browser computation has deliberate limits. Use corridor-sized inputs, review budget messages and keep unknown values visible. Regional terrain supports broad screening; site-level estimates need appropriate checked ground and complete sections. The current workspace supports preliminary planning and geometric review, while construction decisions require the appropriate field, engineering and authorization process. [1,2,15]

blocks.title: A pilot with measurable acceptance
blocks.lead: Use one representative access problem with enough complexity to test the intended value: a block or landing, at least two credible alternatives, a known road tie-in, material supply assumptions and a real terrain delivery.

blocks.text: Name a forestry reviewer and the person responsible for data preparation. Agree the scope and tolerances before interpreting results.

rows: Data intake
Every input has a recorded provider, date, CRS, height reference and units. No unexplained terrain mismatch remains.
Terrain support
The accepted road and section reach have no unresolved analytical gaps in quantities being compared. Independent spot checks meet the agreed tolerance.
Alternatives
At least two options use a documented common basis. The reviewer can explain their geometry, quantity and cost differences.
Cost completeness
Required rates and source assumptions are attributable. Unknowns are identified. Reused access and material paths connect under the agreed policy.
Restoration and exchange
The project reopens with the accepted state. Selected GIS/design exports match checked coordinates, units and sample records.
User workflow
A forester completes an agreed edit and review exercise. Issues, time required and assistance are recorded for the adoption decision.

blocks.text: These are proposed pilot criteria, not claimed performance results. The project team should set tolerances appropriate to the source quality and intended planning decision. The pilot report should record any failed criterion, its consequence and the work needed to resolve it, rather than treating an incomplete estimate as a complete price.
What the pilot should produce

A useful handoff contains the accepted source register, editable project, comparison of alternatives, review drawings and schedules, a record of remaining field questions and the selected open exports. It should also identify which requests are configuration, which need development and who will maintain the data.

Measure value against the team's existing process: time to prepare a comparable option, number of manual transfers, clarity of assumptions and ease of reconstructing a decision. Record a baseline and observed pilot results before making a savings claim. A successful outcome is a demonstrably useful planning workflow with a clear boundary between the desktop decision and the next professional task.

blocks.title: Browser use and field readiness
blocks.lead: The core road workflow runs in the browser. Geometry, quantities, route searches, drainage calculations and bounded point-cloud preparation execute locally, including worker-based processing where implemented. [1,16]

blocks.text: A separate CAD or GIS application or a per-user processing server is not required for those calculations. Network access still matters for obtaining the application, source terrain, public records and background mapping.
The same workspace at a smaller screen size

The responsive interface exposes plan and profile through pane tabs and reveals editing controls on demand. A live check at a 414 by 896 pixel viewport confirmed these controls with a synthetic training example. This was a browser viewport check, not a physical-phone field trial or a measured large-LiDAR performance test. Local projects use browser storage; portable project files provide a deliberate handoff between devices. They do not automatically synchronize edits. [16]

rows: Local calculations
Core design and analysis run locally once the required application code and inputs are present. Test the agreed project size and edit sequence on the intended device.
Project portability
Imported terrain grids can travel with the project. Native published terrain is restored from a source URL and hash in a fresh session, so a project file is not always a complete offline package.
Installed appearance
A web-app manifest and production service worker are implemented. End-to-end installation, updates and reopening must be checked on the target browser and operating system.
Disconnected work
The current worker caches selected same-origin resources. External basemaps and live services remain separate dependencies; regional terrain caching is bounded and temporary.

blocks.text: Scope an offline delivery around the actual project

A reliable disconnected deployment requires deliberate packaging: application JavaScript, workers, WASM, terrain, relevant context and permitted basemap data must all be available locally. The regional terrain cache has a 128-tile limit and a seven-day age policy; it is not a permanent project archive. Downloaded project files remain the durable handoff. For a field pilot, test installation, a network-isolated cold start, project reopening, plan/profile navigation, an agreed edit, recalculation and export on the actual devices. Complete offline operation is a proposed acceptance outcome, not a blanket guarantee of the current public deployment. [10,16]

blocks.title: How DDC Access fits the available choices
blocks.lead: DDC Access offers a particular combination: BC access evidence, terrain preparation, interactive road alternatives and explicit assumptions in a browser workspace.

blocks.text: A purchase decision should consider that workflow alongside the engineering software, specialist datasets and professional services the organization already uses. blocks.text: Acknowledge the overlap

LiDAR, linked views, drainage, road networks and customization are not exclusive DDC Access capabilities. Softree documents GPS-enabled Windows-tablet use, an iPad/iPhone field-entry app, offline network-licence checkout, an optimization API and custom template services. These offerings have their own licence and support conditions. [17-22]

Forsite combines remote sensing with field-calibrated inventory and professional forestry work. Exchange also describes offline field maps for Avenza. Its current catalogue marks DEM and canopy-height products available, field maps available in some areas, and several other layers coming soon. Confirm coverage and product availability for the actual site. [23-26]
Evaluate the combination on one representative job

A practical pilot can bring the forester and technical reviewer into the same discussion: locate the access problem, prepare appropriate ground, compare a small set of alternatives and inspect the assumptions behind each result. Specialist data or established design tools may remain part of the handoff. Any connection to a named vendor must be scoped and checked; no prebuilt Forsite connector or commercial partnership is implied.

Use common terrain, constraints, rates and deliverables when comparing options. Measure preparation time, revision effort, unresolved issues and export acceptance. The intended result is a useful planning workflow for the customer; this paper makes no claim of lower price, superior accuracy or guaranteed savings.
